documents.abstract: As flexible major selection systems, including undeclared admission, become increasingly widespread in higher education, learners' capacity for self-directed academic and career planning has become more important than ever.Although the widespread adoption of Generative AI (GenAI) has improved the efficiency of information acquisition, it also raises concerns about intensified cognitive offloading, whereby learners become overly dependent on AI-generated responses without engaging in critical thinking.To address this issue, this study proposes an AI-based integrated metacognitive scaffolding model that enables learners to use AI not merely as an information provider, but as a tool for expanding their thinking.To this end, an integrative literature review explored the theoretical relationship between metacognition and scaffolding, and a cross-mapping analysis was used to derive stage-specific design principles.In addition, a scenario-based walkthrough examined the logical applicability of the proposed model.The analysis suggests that AI-supported major exploration can be conceptually organized around the role of an Inquiring Coach.The proposed model organizes the learning process into three metacognitive phases-Planning, Monitoring, and Evaluation-and specifies stage-specific strategies, including delaying immediate answers, detecting inconsistencies and generating counter-questions, and promoting reflective self-explanation.The model also incorporates a Fading mechanism as a design principle intended to support the gradual development of learners' selfdirected exploration.This study provides conceptual design guidelines for AI-supported career education systems.It proposes a theoretical basis for shifting attention from information-delivery efficiency to designing interactions that support learners' thinking.However, the model's effects on learners' metacognition or career decision-making were not empirically tested.

Search-and-rescue (SAR) drone swarms increasingly require multi-operator supervision, in which backup behaviors redistribute cognitive load to improve performance but introduce trade-offs in situational awareness (SA) and task engagement. Existing human-autonomy teaming interfaces present symmetric displays across all roles, ignoring the asymmetric information needs of backup providers and recipients. We developed a two-human, eight-drone Unity SAR testbed that operationalizes three team structures (independent, Operator A-busy, Operator B-busy) via event-allocation manipulation, with a SPAM (Situation Present Assessment Method)-derived in-task SA probe. Three iterative focus groups with eight human-centered design researchers and professionals yielded four display conditions: no-display baseline, effort display, urgency display, and combined. Semi-structured interviews with three SAR practitioners confirmed high realism ratings for the overall testbed and the viability of dynamic backup. A feasibility pilot study ( N = 4) revealed a significant main effect of team structure on backup count, confirming that the manipulation elicits backup behaviors as designed.

Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) changes digital retail from consumer-led search to delegated decision making, increasing both the potential value and the agency risks of recommendation. This conceptual article asks the following: Under what architectural and governance conditions can an autonomous shopping agent earn calibrated consumer trust while supporting economically and environmentally appropriate consumption decisions? Using a purposive, multidisciplinary synthesis of signaling theory, principal–agent theory, the ability–benevolence–integrity model of trust, trustworthy AI, recommender system governance, and sustainable consumption research, we develop a process model linking four architectural features to consumer perceptions, delegation, reliance, and decision outcomes. The features are scoped provenance verification, disclosed and audited commercial incentives, faithful contrastive explanations, and active evaluation of retention, repair, refurbishment, and purchase. We argue that justified non-purchase advice can function as a credible signal of consumer alignment only when the operator is the signal sender, the advice creates observable opportunity or accountability costs, and compensation and audit arrangements make imitation more costly for a misaligned operator. The framework distinguishes perceived trustworthiness from overall trust, willingness to delegate, actual reliance, recommendation appropriateness, and lifecycle sustainability. A five-layer architecture, a worked decision example, and four testable propositions specify how missing data, conflicting preferences, uncertainty, authorization, privacy, and accountability should be handled. This article treats the applications as illustrations rather than empirical cases and concludes with limitations and an empirical research agenda focused on calibrated—not merely increased—trust.

documents.abstract: Abstract Performing manual tasks involves ergonomic risk factors associated with musculoskeletal disorders. This paper presents an adaptive workstation designed to adjust the working height according to individual anthropometric characteristics and evaluates its effects on posture, perceived strain, and the duration of value-adding activities. The study examined abstracted manual tasks with relevance to end-of-life vehicle disassembly. A proof-of-concept study with twelve participants shows that more frequent height adjustments reduce exposure to ergonomically unfavorable joint-angle ranges and perceived strain without significantly affecting the duration of value-adding activities. Adaptive systems therefore have the potential to reduce awkward postures in end-of-life vehicle disassembly. The findings should be examined in a dedicated disassembly use case, taking into account varying product conditions and appropriate positioning of the work object for tasks requiring high force exertion. Practical Relevance : This paper presents an adaptive workstation that can be adjusted for various (dis-)assembly and maintenance applications. The findings of the proof-of-concept study suggest that adaptive systems offer prospects for reducing physical stress and strain during manual tasks.

documents.abstract: Abstract Digital transformation is increasingly important for firms seeking to remain resilient under conditions of uncertainty, yet less is known about how digital technologies strengthen resilience when they are embedded in specific operating routines. This study examines whether digital cash-to-cash transformation, the digital redesign and operational integration of inventory, receivables, and payables routines, enhances organisational resilience. Using Chinese listed firms from 2012 to 2024, we construct a large-language-model-based textual measure from annual reports that distinguishes substantive digital transformation in working-capital processes from generic digital disclosure. The results show that digital cash-to-cash transformation is positively associated with a multidimensional measure of organisational resilience. This finding remains robust to alternative measures, instrumental-variable estimation, propensity score matching, double machine learning, and shock-based tests. Mechanism analyses indicate that the resilience benefits of digital transformation arise primarily through working-capital buffer configuration rather than simple cash-cycle compression. Specifically, digital transformation is associated with higher inventory, receivables, and payables postures, each of which is positively related to resilience. The effects are stronger among more focused firms and firms pursuing differentiation strategies. These findings suggest that the resilience value of digital transformation lies not merely in adopting digital technologies, but in embedding them in cash-to-cash routines that improve information visibility, coordination, and the flexible deployment of working-capital resources.

This research presents a literature review that investigates how digital competencies relate to student engagement, particularly in the integration of deep learning in primary education. Drawing on findings from a diverse range of peer-reviewed studies published between 2018 and 2025, this review highlights that digital proficiency, including digital literacy, skills, and creativity, is closely associated with students’ cognitive, emotional, and behavioral engagement. The effective use of digital resources, such as artificial intelligence, virtual reality, and adaptive learning systems, promotes critical thinking and facilitates deep learning. The findings show that students with advanced digital capabilities demonstrate greater concentration and enthusiasm, whereas those with limited skills and autonomy are more likely to disengage and exhibit off-task behaviors online. Additional factors, such as personalized learning, social and emotional engagement, and teacher’s digital expertise also influence this relationship. Identified challenges include digital disparities, insufficient teacher preparation, and distractions from non-educational digital activities. To address these challenges, targeted digital literacy initiatives and improvements in curriculum design are recommended. In summary, this review highlights the complex relationship between digital competencies and student engagement, emphasizing the importance of comprehensive curriculum integration and teacher support to enhance learning outcomes through deep learning approaches in primary education.

This study assessed the digital technology utilization of junior high school students at Lataban National High School, Liloan, Cebu, during School Year 2025–2026 as the basis for developing a Digitization Model. Anchored in constructivist, connectivist, academic learning, and literacy-development perspectives, the study employed a descriptive-correlational research design involving 75 Grade 9 and Grade 10 students selected through total enumeration. Data were gathered using an adapted questionnaire and analyzed through frequencies, percentages, weighted means, standard deviations, and Pearson product-moment correlation. Findings revealed that respondents demonstrated very high technological skills (M = 4.24) and high levels of personal security, critical thinking, device security, informational, and communication skills. Digital tool utilization was high in online collaboration (M = 4.12), artificial intelligence in education (M = 3.96), electronic boards for learning (M = 3.42), and excessive technology use (M = 3.82). Internet resources (M = 3.50) and open-source AI tools (M = 3.42) showed high availability, while AI subscriptions (M = 3.19) and laptops (M = 3.29) demonstrated moderate availability. A significant positive relationship was established between digital technology utilization skills and digital tool utilization (r = 0.62, p < 0.05), resulting in the rejection of the null hypothesis. The study recommended strengthening digital competencies, improving technological resources, promoting responsible AI utilization, and progressively implementing the proposed Digitization Model. The research supports Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 4 on Quality Education, SDG 9 on Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure, and SDG 10 on Reduced Inequalities. Its sustainability implications involve promoting equitable digital learning opportunities, responsible technology utilization, and evidence-based institutional improvements toward inclusive and sustainable educational digitalization.

This registration documents a scoping review examining how artificial intelligence (AI) disclosure and transparency are conceptualized, operationalized, and evaluated across human-AI communication contexts. The review focuses on four analytically distinct transparency objects: source disclosure, identity disclosure, authorship disclosure, and algorithmic transparency. The review maps disclosure strategies, communication and psychological mechanisms, contextual boundary conditions, user outcomes, methodological characteristics, and evidence gaps. Particular attention is given to trust, credibility, authenticity, social presence, perceived transparency, psychological reactance, mind perception, legitimacy, engagement, acceptance, and related behavioral outcomes. The review follows a Population-Concept-Context (PCC) eligibility framework and draws on literature identified through Scopus and Web of Science Core Collection. Searches were conducted on 28 October 2026 using terms related to artificial intelligence, human-AI communication, and AI disclosure or transparency. After database filtering and deduplication, 146 unique records were screened and 20 sources were included in the final evidence map, comprising 17 primary empirical studies, two secondary syntheses, and one conceptual or perspective article. Findings are synthesized descriptively and thematically and are further organized through a Disclosure-Context-Mechanism-Outcome (DCMO) framework. The framework conceptualizes AI disclosure as a communication process in which disclosure characteristics acquire meaning within specific contexts, activate interpretive mechanisms, and produce different evaluative or behavioral outcomes. This OSF registration is retrospective. The literature search, screening, data charting, methodological appraisal, evidence synthesis, and initial manuscript preparation had already been completed before registration. The record is therefore intended to provide a transparent and time-stamped account of the review methods and should not be interpreted as a prospective preregistration.

With the deep integration of digitalization and artificial intelligence technologies into enterprise knowledge management, AI-assisted learning is reshaping the channels through which knowledge is acquired within organizations. Meanwhile, knowledge dissemination is evolving from traditional interpersonal interaction toward human-machine collaborative interaction. In light of this transformation, this study develops a multi-stage 2 SEIR - CA dynamic model of knowledge dissemination under an AI-enabled mechanism that incorporates dual-channel “interpersonal–human-machine” interaction. Specifically, employees are classified into five states: employees who have not yet mastered the knowledge, employees with limited knowledge mastery, employees with strong knowledge mastery, knowledge-disseminating employees, and knowledge-exited employees. On this basis, the next-generation matrix method is employed to calculate the basic reproduction number of the system and to analyze the existence and stability of equilibrium points. An optimal control model is then established to derive strategies for promoting knowledge dissemination, and a cellular automaton model is introduced to characterize its spatiotemporal evolution. The results show that the system exhibits a pronounced threshold effect: when key dissemination parameters exceed their critical levels, knowledge can continue to diffuse within the organization; otherwise, it will gradually decay. Second, the AI-enabled mechanism enhances knowledge transformation efficiency and contact intensity, thereby significantly promoting the transition of employees with strong knowledge mastery to knowledge-disseminating employees. Third, the optimal control strategy proposed in this study can optimize transformation pathways across different stages under resource constraints, thereby improving overall dissemination efficiency and maintaining the structural stability of the dissemination system. Fourth, the spatiotemporal simulations demonstrate that, under optimal regulation, knowledge dissemination can form a stable diffusion pattern with high coverage. Under the assumptions and parameter settings of the proposed model, the findings provide theoretical insights into the dynamic mechanisms underlying AI-enabled knowledge dissemination and offer model-based implications for knowledge management practices in organizations.

documents.abstract: Occupational hazards, injuries, work-related illnesses, and fatalities remain core public health challenges in industrial settings. Workers in oilseed processing factories are exposed to multiple occupational risks; however, evidence regarding the effectiveness of occupational health and safety educational interventions in these settings remains limited and not explored and examined. The main objective of this study is to evaluate the effect of educational program on workers occupational health and safety (OHS) knowledge, attitudes, practices, and the prevalence of occupational injuries in oilseed processing (OSP) factories. A quasi-experimental controlled pretest–posttest intervention study design will be conducted among 466 factory workers selected through simple random sampling and equally allocated to intervention and control groups. Around 466 workers recruited from 10 randomly selected OSP factories in Eastern Ethiopia. The factories will be purposively allocated into intervention (n = 5) and control (n = 5) groups based on geographical location, with 233 workers randomly selected from each group (1:1 allocation). Eligible participants will be factory workers aged ≥18 years with at least one year of employment. OHS Educational intervention program will be implemented for 3 months. The intervention consisted of a three-month OHS educational program incorporating health education sessions, on-the-job training, and informational leaflets. Data will be collected at baseline and post-intervention. Data will be entered using Epi-Data and analyzed in STATA version 16.1. Between-group differences will be assessed using chi-square, independent t-, and Mann-Whitney tests. Multivariable logistic regression and generalized estimating equations (GEE) will be applied to estimate intervention effects using a difference-in-differences approach. Statistical significance will be set at p < 0.05. Regarding ethics and dissemination, Ethical approval was obtained from the Jimma University Institute of Health Institutional Review Board (Ref: JUIH/IRPB/217/25). Findings will be disseminated through collaboration with factory management, health professionals, government agencies, community stakeholders, and non-governmental organizations to facilitate the implementation and scale-up of effective workplace OHS interventions. This study will generate robust evidence on the effectiveness of an OHS educational program in enhancing workers OHS knowledge, attitudes, and practices while reducing or not occupational injuries and work-related Musculo-skeletal disorders (WMSDs) among OSP factories workers in Ethiopia. The study is expected to generate context-specific evidence that can inform workplace OHS policies and guide the development of feasible, evidence-based interventions for industrial workers in Ethiopia. At the time of reporting, the intervention is started but not completed, and post-intervention data collection is also not completed.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Employee well-being has is no longer viewed only as an employee-support activity to becoming an important component of strategic human resource management. Apparently many organizations are increasingly investing in employee assistance programmes, mental-health support, flexible work, health promotion, financial well-being, manager training, occupational health, and other interventions. The focus managerial question, however, is whether these programmes produce measurable equitable financial returns. So this article examines that question critically by distinguishing return on investment (ROI) from broader organizational value, reviewing evidence on absenteeism, presenteeism, turnover, productivity, engagement, health costs and organizational performance, and identifying the methodological difficulties involved in attributing business outcomes to well-being interventions. The evidences lament that well-designed programs can generate measurable benefits, but a positive financial ROI should not be assumed. Results vary subsequently according to intervention type, implementation quality, work force characteristics, and time horizon and evaluation design. Systematic reviews provide a blended picture in a way that some workplace prevention interventions report positive economic outcomes, while higher-quality studies of some wellness programs have found little or zero short-term financial ROI. This means that Human Resource professionals should avoid treating well-being as either an automatic cost or a source of savings. Instead, organizations should identify the specific workforce problem, select evidence-informed interventions, establish baseline measures, use comparison groups where possible, calculate total program costs, and evaluate outcomes over an appropriate period of time. The article concludes with an HR evaluation framework that integrates financial ROI with employee, operational and strategic measures. It also discusses different implications for organizations in developing economies, including Uganda, where resource constraints make evidence-based prioritization particularly important.

Epistemic game theory explains an agent's strategic behavior via the beliefs it holds about others and how these beliefs are updated as the interactions unfold. Modern LLM-based agents, however, often lack an explicit mechanism for learning and updating such beliefs to guide decisions under incomplete information. To bridge this gap, we propose EpiAgent, a framework that equips LLM-based agents with an explicit, learnable epistemic layer, which maintains beliefs over others' private information and combines these beliefs with the agent's available information into an epistemic state for action selection. Concretely, the agent's policy is decomposed into two coupled stages: Epistemic Update, which updates these beliefs from interaction histories, and Action Planning, which selects actions conditioned on the updated epistemic state. By formulating their dependency as a bi-level optimization problem, we introduce Epistemic Self-Play, an algorithm that alternately optimizes the two stages through self-play, utilizing an intrinsic prediction reward to evaluate how well inferred beliefs predict subsequent observations. Empirical results across both mixed and competitive scenarios show that EpiAgent consistently outperforms prompting-based and RL-based baselines. Further analyses reveal the benefits of dedicated epistemic training, improvements in belief inference accuracy, and the contribution of learned beliefs to action planning. These results demonstrate the value of an explicit, learnable epistemic layer for effective multi-agent interactions.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly reshaping teaching, learning, and knowledge production in higher education. However, limited attention has been given to justice-oriented frameworks that connect AI-mediated education with epistemic agency and critical consciousness, particularly within market-driven university contexts. This conceptual article explores how teaching can be reimagined to cultivate epistemic agency and critical consciousness in AI-mediated higher education through a justice-oriented pedagogical framework. The article draws on frameworks such as critical pedagogy, decolonial theory, and epistemic justice to foreground the findings of this research. It employs a narrative-integrative review methodology to synthesise contemporary scholarship on AI and social justice in higher education. The article argues for a shift beyond transmissive and instrumental models of learning towards relational pedagogies that position learners as active co-creators of knowledge. It examines how AI technologies may reinforce or disrupt epistemic hierarchies through algorithmic bias, automated decision-making, and changing processes of knowledge production. The original contribution is a justice-oriented conceptual framework that integrates pedagogical design, institutional cultures, power relations, and technological systems for a better education experience. It recommends embedding critical AI literacy across curricula and aligning pedagogy with principles of epistemic justice to support equitable and socially transformative higher education in an increasingly algorithmic world.

Artificial intelligence is playing a great role in the production, classification, retrieval, and communication of knowledge. Tools like large language models, recommender systems, automated decision-making systems, and search engines do more than just process information; they shape whose testimony is heard, which concepts become available for interpreting experience, and which claims are treated as credible or important. This paper argues that Miranda Fricker's theory of epistemic injustice offers a strong framework to ethically identify shortcomings in AI-enabled knowledge production; however, it also suggests that, the distinction made in classical accounts between testimonial and hermeneutical injustices needs to be extended in order to address them in the context of sociotechnical systems. Testimonial injustice can arise when algorithmic models reproduce credibility deficits through biased training data, proxy variables, ranking practices, moderation systems, or automated classification. On the other hand, hermeneutical injustice can emerge when certain communities are poorly represented in the conceptual and linguistic tools that AI systems use to create explanations, categories, and interpretations. The paper further argues that the opaque nature of many AI systems intensifies these harms because affected persons may be unable to understand, contest, or correct the epistemic processes that affect them. Building on Fricker, Floridi, Dotson, Medina, and contemporary work in AI ethics, the paper develops an epistemic justice framework centred on adequacy in represantation, credibility protection, interpretive inclusion, contestability, provenance, and institutional accountability. The proposed framework treats epistemic justice not merely as a desirable output property but as a design and governance requirement for AI systems that participate in consequential knowledge practices.

Dear Editor The increasing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into healthcare systems has introduced both technological advancement and ethical transformation in nursing practice. While AI-based tools enhance clinical efficiency, documentation accuracy, and decision-support processes, their ethical implications regarding patient privacy, professional accountability, and ethical decision-making remain critically debated. In this systematic examination of empirical studies published between 2015 and 2025, key ethical dimensions of AI application in nursing were analyzed. Findings indicate persistent concerns about data confidentiality, ambiguity in responsibility boundaries, and potential over-reliance on algorithmic recommendations. At the same time, AI-assisted education demonstrates positive effects on ethical reasoning and professional self-awareness. However, the absence of clear governance frameworks and explicit accountability policies limits the safe and ethically grounded implementation of AI in nursing practice. Strengthening digital ethics education, clarifying shared accountability between clinicians and intelligent systems, and conducting longitudinal clinical research are essential priorities for advancing ethical AI integration in nursing.

documents.abstract: Conversational interfaces may make explainable AI (XAI) more accessible to users without machine learning expertise, but their benefits over dashboards remain insufficiently characterised in healthcare. Existing systems have typically been evaluated in isolation, leaving unclear whether conversational interaction improves interpretability beyond the underlying explanation methods. We report a within-subjects user study comparing the Explainability Assistant, an LLM function-calling conversational XAI system, with a traditional dashboard for explaining a heart disease classification model trained on the Cleveland Heart Disease dataset. Both interfaces expose the same Decision Tree classifier and post-hoc explanation methods: SHAP feature attribution, DiCE counterfactuals, and what-if analysis. This design supports comparison of interaction modalities while holding the model and explanation methods constant. Five participants with healthcare backgrounds, from medical students to practising clinicians and public health researchers, completed parallel task blocks on both interfaces; three participated in follow-up interviews. Task accuracy, Likert ratings, free-text questionnaire responses, and interviews revealed complementary strengths and weaknesses rather than a clear preference for either modality. The assistant offered easier entry and patient-specific explanations, while the dashboard supported simultaneous inspection of global and local information. All three interview participants recommended integrating conversational and dashboard elements within a single clinical workflow.

documents.abstract: ABSTRACT Introduction. Burnout represents a significant occupational health concern among healthcare professionals. The present study estimated the prevalence of burnout and examined its associated socio-demographic and occupational factors in the Souss-Massa region of Morocco. Methods: A multicenter cross-sectional study was conducted from November 2025 to January 2026 among 462 professionals employed in public healthcare institutions across the six provinces of the region. Burnout was measured using the French version of the Maslach Burnout Inventory–Human Services Survey. Associations between burnout and potential factors were examined using bivariate analyses, with statistical significance defined as p ≤ 0.05. Results: The prevalence of at least one dimension of burnout was 82.3%, while 12.6% of participants exhibited all three dimensions concurrently. High levels of emotional exhaustion and depersonalization were observed in 67.3% and 39.0% of participants, respectively. Regarding personal accomplishment, 33.1% reported low levels, 21.4% moderate levels, and 45.5% high levels. Significant associations were observed with marital status, number of children, educational level, occupation, province of practice, type of healthcare setting, and working arrangements (p < 0.001). The presence of chronic illness (p = 0.003), overtime (p = 0.035), and working more than ten hours a day at least once a week (p = 0.018) were also significantly associated with burnout. Conclusion: Burnout was highly prevalent, with emotional exhaustion as the most common dimension. These findings underscore the necessity for targeted organizational interventions to safeguard the healthcare professionals in the workplace.RESUMEIntroduction. Le burnout constitue un problème majeur de santé au travail chez les professionnels de santé. Cette étude a estimé la prévalence du burnout et examiné les facteurs sociodémographiques et professionnels associés dans la région Souss-Massa au Maroc. Méthodes. Nous avons mené une étude transversale multicentrique de novembre 2025 à janvier 2026 auprès de 462 professionnels exerçant dans des établissements publics de santé des six provinces de la région. Nous avons mesuré le burnout à l'aide de la version française du Maslach Burnout Inventory–Human Services Survey, comprenant 22 items répartis en trois dimensions : épuisement émotionnel (EE), dépersonnalisation (DP) et accomplissement personnel (AP). Nous avons utilisé des analyses bivariées pour examiner les associations, avec un seuil de significativité fixé à p ≤ 0,05. Résultats. La prévalence d'au moins une dimension du burnout était de 82,3 % ; 12,6 % des participants présentaient les trois dimensions. Un niveau élevé d'EE était identifié chez 67,3 % des participants, une DP élevée chez 39,0 % et un faible AP chez 33,1 %. Des associations significatives ont été observées avec le statut matrimonial, le nombre d'enfants, le niveau d'études, la profession, la province d'exercice, le type d'établissement et le régime de travail (p < 0,001). La présence d'une maladie chronique (p = 0,003), les heures supplémentaires (p = 0,035) et le travail de plus de dix heures par jour au moins une fois par semaine (p = 0,018) étaient également significativement associés au burnout. L'âge, le sexe, le tabagisme et l'activité physique n'étaient pas associés. Conclusion. Le burnout était très prévalent dans cette région, avec l'épuisement émotionnel comme dimension dominante. Les infirmiers, les travailleurs postés et les professionnels des hôpitaux provinciaux étaient les plus affectés. Ces résultats appellent à des interventions organisationnelles ciblées pour protéger les professionnels de santé au Souss-Massa.

Abstract Background: Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) is increasingly proposed as a way to make clinical decision-support systems more transparent and acceptable to healthcare professionals. However, explanation does not necessarily improve clinical decisions: it may help users identify relevant evidence, have no measurable effect, or encourage excessive reliance on incorrect AI advice. This review synthesises empirical evidence on how clinician-facing explanations influence trust, reliance, and decision quality. Methods: A structured evidence search was conducted on 20 October 2026 using web-indexed scholarly search, PubMed/PMC records, and publisher-hosted full-text pages. Search concepts combined explainable AI, clinical decision support, clinicians/physicians, trust/reliance, diagnostic accuracy, and human-AI decision-making. A core set of ten empirical studies was identified and characterised from the study table and reference list of Rosenbacke et al. (2024), with key primary reports checked against publisher or PubMed records. More recent evidence was used to contextualise the findings. Because a complete exportable database search and independent duplicate screening were not available in this workflow, this is a transparent structured systematic evidence synthesis rather than a fully reproducible database-level review; no new PRISMA record counts are claimed. Results: The evidence indicates that explanations can improve perceived understandability and sometimes support decision performance, but their effects on trust are inconsistent and context-dependent. In a chemotherapy decision-support experiment involving 41 medical practitioners, example-based and counterfactual explanations were easier to understand than some alternatives, yet explanations also increased willingness to accept AI recommendations, including incorrect ones. In an X-ray experiment involving 223 physicians, annotated AI advice improved diagnostic accuracy particularly for non-radiology experts, while confidence in clinicians' own diagnoses did not meaningfully change. Other studies reported increased trust or intention to use AI, no clear effect, or concerns about complex, irrelevant, or time-consuming explanations. Conclusion: XAI should not be evaluated by whether it increases trust alone. Evaluation should test whether clinicians can distinguish correct from incorrect recommendations, whether reliance is appropriately calibrated, and whether explanations fit clinical workflows. Larger, preregistered, multisite studies using realistic clinical tasks and common outcome measures are needed.

documents.abstract: The Analog Electronic Technology course is concept-intensive, and its circuit analysis methods are flexible. A relatively common difficulty among students is that “single-point knowledge can still be mastered, but the overall context is difficult to connect.” In teaching, problems such as linear content organization, unified learning support, a long feedback cycle, and mismatch between resources and needs have existed for a long time. In response, this study takes Outcome-Based Education (OBE) as the basic guidance, connects the structured organization ability of the smart knowledge graph with the dialogue interaction ability of the artificial intelligence (AI) agent, and constructs a blended teaching model driven by an AI smart knowledge graph. Starting from graduation requirements and course objectives, knowledge points are reversely decomposed, four types of associations, namely prerequisite, parallel, causal, and application associations, are sorted out, and a three-layer smart knowledge graph organized in five levels of “course-module-chapter-knowledge point-sub-knowledge point” is formed. On this basis, an AI teaching agent is developed to undertake preview guidance, in-class question answering, homework correction, learning situation analysis, and other work. The teaching process is then rearranged according to the three stages of before class, in class, and after class. A one-semester comparative practice shows that the final average score of the experimental class is 8.7 points higher than that of the control class, the score difference in comprehensive questions is especially obvious, the proportion of students independently completing design experiments has increased, and the dispersion of scores has also narrowed. The relevant practices have certain reference value for the intelligent transformation of basic courses in electronic information majors, but the scope of application of the conclusions is still limited by the sample size and implementation rounds.

Introduction: Artificial intelligence (AI) offers opportunities to improve the efficiency of healthcare, but its integration in sub-Saharan Africa faces structural constraints. This exploratory study analyzes the perceptions, expectations, and fears of healthcare professionals in the Ibanda Health Zone (Bukavu, DRC) to document the professional acceptability of these technologies. Methods: The study used a mixed-methods approach: the qualitative exploratory component was based on semi-structured interviews with 11 professionals (physicians, nurses, technicians, managers). The data underwent inductive thematic analysis supplemented by descriptive frequency quantification. Results: Overall attitudes toward AI are favorable, albeit with certain conditions. Despite a predominantly basic or informal understanding of AI (81.8%), perceived benefits include improved diagnostics (72.7%) and data management (63.6%). However, major obstacles persist: lack of formal training (81.8%), internet instability (72.7%), and concerns about the reliability of results (54.5%). AI acceptance is high but conditional, revealing a gap between technological promises and realities on the ground. Training (cited by 90.9% of participants) emerges as the central lever and an ethical prerequisite for safe use. Conclusion : The integration of AI at Ibanda cannot be reduced to a technical issue; it requires strengthening basic infrastructure, a clear regulatory framework, and active involvement of caregivers in the design of tools.

documents.abstract: This study, grounded in the psychology of working theory (PWT) and self-determination theory (SDT), examined how working conditions shape musicians’ experiences of decent work, intrinsic motivation, artistic identity, creative engagement, and psychological well-being. Sixteen in-depth interviews were conducted with Portuguese musicians, including both freelancers and those with stable contracts. Reflexive thematic analysis identified four overarching themes: (a) job security and precarity, (b) intrinsic motivation, autonomy, and creative engagement, (c) artistic identity and purpose, and (d) well-being and mental health. The findings show that freelance instability undermines security, constrains creative risk-taking, and increases stress, whereas financial and institutional stability supports intrinsic motivation, reinforces artistic identity, and enables creative exploration. Features associated with intrinsic motivation, voluntary engagement, persistence, and psychological investment in creative tasks were observed across both groups. Autonomy itself sustained engagement for some freelancers, highlighting personal resilience and self-directed creativity. The results underscore the interplay between structural conditions (PWT) and individual motivations (SDT), showing that sustainable work environments foster well-being and high-quality creative output. The study provides practical implications for policies, education, and organizational strategies to support healthier, more productive artistic ecosystems.

This qualitative descriptive study explored how nurse educators at Olivarez College Tagaytay, Cavite, accepted and integrated generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in nursing education and developed an evidence-informed action plan. Eight purposively selected nurse educators who had used GenAI in teaching participated in semi-structured, in-depth interviews during August 2026. The interview guide was expert-validated, and recordings were transcribed and examined through Braun and Clarke’s six-phase thematic analysis. Data collection occurred in three waves; 125 codes were organized into six themes and 16 subthemes. The themes were unplanned entry into a necessary technology; conditional acceptance anchored in professional judgment; adapting under generational pressure; integration at the preparation stage; safeguarding learning through vigilance and assessment redesign; and enablement by leadership without written policy. Educators perceived GenAI as useful for preparing lessons, cases, questions, and simplified learning materials but insisted on verifying outputs and protecting clinical judgment, empathy, academic integrity, and patient safety. Integration remained largely preparatory and individualized, while participants described uneven digital confidence, assessment vulnerabilities, personal subscription costs, and the absence of consistent written rules despite administrative encouragement. The findings indicate a gap between conditional acceptance and systematic pedagogical integration. A five-component action plan addressing governance, differentiated faculty development, assessment integrity, student AI literacy, and technical access was proposed, not evaluated. The study contributes institution-specific evidence to responsible GenAI adoption in nursing education.

documents.abstract: Abstract Research on large language model failure predominantly assesses models in single exchanges and isolation: a prompted model, a scored output, and a reported error rate. The focus on single exchanges and isolation belies these current models’ professional use. Clinicians, attorneys, analysts, educators, and researchers work across extended sessions, and each output becomes the context for the next, while the final product carries a human signature. A test that scores a single response most likely will not reveal the behaviors that emerge under those conditions. This paper describes seven candidate failure patterns identified in exploratory, single-author observation of extended sessions on three commercial AI platforms: recognition without correction, compounding rather than isolation of errors, halo effect from real anchors, unreliable self-explanation, degradation across long sessions, exculpatory framing under confrontation, and sycophancy and confirmation bias amplification. Several are consistent with findings already established in the machine learning literature. Overall, the patterns describe a systemic failure profile that lower hallucination rates do not address because the concern lies in how the system handles errors once they exist. The systemic failure profile carries significant ethical consequences and concerns, since failures cascade to final approval; the duty to verify applies to any domain where a person approves LLM output.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Background: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is now part of routine academic work in health professions education, often outpacing institutional policy, infrastructure, and training. We describe how educators and trainees use GenAI, their concerns, and the institutional support they perceive, and examine whether prior AI training and frequency of use are associated with these perceptions. Methods: We conducted a cross-sectional online survey (August–November 2025) of faculty, clinicians, staff, and trainees involved in health professions education across the United States, recruited through professional networks. Ten items on a 0–5 agreement scale captured attitudes, concerns, trust in AI accuracy, and perceived institutional resources. We used descriptive statistics, Spearman correlations, Mann–Whitney U tests with Holm correction, and multivariable ordinal logistic regression with sensitivity analyses. Results: Of 211 responses, 183 respondents with documented consent were analyzed (76.5% faculty; 48 named institutions). Nearly all had used GenAI (98.9%), and 78.1% used it at least weekly, most often for writing or editing (77.6%). Half or more agreed or strongly agreed that they were concerned about academic integrity (58.5%), data privacy (56.3%), and professional accountability (50.8%), yet only 14.2% agreed or strongly agreed that they trust the accuracy of AI-generated content. Only 24.0% agreed or strongly agreed that their institution provides the resources they need (M = 2.51). Among respondents with elevated concern, 73.8% still used GenAI weekly or more. Any AI training (39.9%, mostly informal workshops) was associated with greater comfort and perceived institutional resources, but not significantly with trust or any concern. More frequent use was independently associated with greater trust (OR 4.93, 95% CI 2.46–9.86) and fewer ethical concerns (OR 0.31, 95% CI 0.16–0.61), and both associations held in sensitivity analyses. Privacy concern was not associated with use frequency. Conclusions: GenAI has become part of routine work for most health professions educators, yet it coexists with substantial concerns about privacy, integrity, and accountability. Training was associated with comfort but not with lower concern, suggesting that faculty development alone is unlikely to be sufficient; institutions may need to pair it with the governance, data protection, and approved tools that individual training cannot provide.

documents.abstract: Transformasi ekonomi digital meningkatkan volume, kecepatan, dan kompleksitas informasi yang harus diproses organisasi dalam pengambilan keputusan bisnis. Perkembangan artificial intelligence (AI) kemudian menggeser fungsi teknologi dari sekadar pendukung keputusan menuju penguatan kapasitas kognitif, kolaborasi manusia–AI, dan keterlibatan yang lebih luas dalam proses keputusan. Penelitian ini bertujuan mensintesis perkembangan peran AI dalam pengambilan keputusan bisnis dan mengidentifikasi bagaimana perubahan tersebut membentuk arsitektur pengambilan keputusan baru dalam ekonomi digital. Penelitian menggunakan pendekatan kualitatif melalui qualitative thematic literature review. Penelusuran literatur dilakukan melalui basis data Scopus dan menghasilkan 1.326 rekaman awal, kemudian 1.303 rekaman unik. Setelah penyaringan akses full-text dan relevansi substantif, diperoleh 45 artikel untuk pemeriksaan penuh, dengan 38 artikel ditetapkan sebagai corpus inti. Analisis tematik menghasilkan empat tema utama: (1) pergeseran dari AI decision support menuju AI augmentation; (2) kolaborasi manusia–AI dan rekonstruksi pertimbangan manajerial; (3) perluasan peran generative AI dalam proses pengambilan keputusan; dan (4) trust, governance, serta batas kewenangan keputusan AI. Hasil sintesis menunjukkan bahwa transformasi AI tidak semata-mata mengarah pada penggantian manusia, tetapi pada reorganisasi pembagian kerja kognitif dan kewenangan keputusan antara manusia dan mesin. Berdasarkan temuan tersebut, penelitian mengusulkan konsep AI-Augmented Business Decision Architecture sebagai kerangka untuk memahami transformasi pengambilan keputusan bisnis di era ekonomi digital.

documents.abstract: AI in education is changing faster than conventional academic publishing can follow. A paper that takes a year to reach print may describe tools, policies and evidence that have already been superseded. This article describes an experiment in doing things differently. Over a single evening in October 2026, a practitioner-scholar and an AI agent turned a body of 81 long-form newsletter articles on AI in education into ten thematic papers, each with original figures, verified references and an open disclosure of how it was made, and published them in Future Science Archives, a non-profit, open-review archive. The article sets out the motivation for the experiment, including the author's long interest in educational innovation and his concerns about the economics of academ‐ ic publishing. It describes the venue and its strengths and limitations, the source corpus, the workflow and the division of labour between human and AI, and the verification process, which found and corrected more than two dozen errors, unverifiable claims and one retracted study carried over from the newsletters. It reports the actual publication timeline. It then discusses the risks of the approach, including "research slop", weakened rigour and researchers becoming editors of machine-written text, and argues that these risks are real but manageable when the human remains responsible for judgement and the process is transparent. It closes with a replicable workflow for others.

Medical education is evolving rapidly alongside the emergence of artificial intelligence (AI) and large language models (LLMs). Continuing medical education (CME) has traditionally relied on educational modalities sometimes conceptualized as the “three P’s” of Posters, Podium presentations, and Publications, later expanded into the “seven P’s” with the addition of Podcasts, Play, Peer-to-peer learning, and Patient interactions. This commentary proposes Prompting as an eighth “P” of CME, reflecting the growing importance of effectively interacting with AI systems in clinical and academic practice. Prompting refers to the process of crafting and refining instructions that guide AI-generated outputs. The quality, specificity, and contextual framing of prompts substantially influence the accuracy and usefulness of responses generated by LLMs. Emerging evidence suggests that prompting is a learnable skill that can improve educational and clinical utility without requiring advanced technical expertise. This commentary reviews key prompting strategies, including zero-shot, few-shot, role-based, chain-of-thought, and iterative prompting, and discusses their relevance to healthcare providers. Applications across clinical care, medical education, patient communication, administration, and research are explored. Potential benefits include generating differential diagnoses, summarizing medical literature, creating educational materials, supporting clinical simulations, and improving patient-facing communication. The commentary also addresses important risks associated with LLM use, including hallucinations, automation bias, and overreliance on AI-generated content. Ultimately, prompting is framed not only as a mechanism for learning through AI systems, but also as a modern medical literacy competency that healthcare providers must actively develop as AI becomes increasingly integrated into healthcare and medical education.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Abstract The widespread adoption of video conferencing (VC) platforms during the COVID-19 pandemic has transformed synchronous higher education, yet sustaining student engagement in such environments remains a persistent challenge, particularly in creative disciplines. This study investigated the effectiveness of three gamification elements included animated badges, experience points, and level upgrades in enhancing behavioural, emotional, and cognitive engagement within a synchronous VC learning context. Guided by Self-Determination Theory (SDT), this study employed a quasi-experimental non-equivalent control group design involving 124 first-year undergraduate graphic design students from three public universities in China. Participants were assigned to a non-gamified control group or one of three gamified conditions and completed pre- and post-intervention surveys measuring multidimensional engagement. Paired t-test analyses revealed statistically significant improvements across all engagement dimensions in the gamified groups (p < 0.001), while the control group exhibited minimal or no meaningful change. Experience points produced the most consistent gains across behavioural, emotional, and cognitive engagement, whereas level upgrades yielded the strongest effects on deep cognitive processing and metacognitive regulation. Animated badges were particularly effective in enhancing emotional engagement and learning enjoyment. One-way ANOVA results further indicated clear performance differentiation between gamified and non-gamified conditions. These findings displayed that well-designed gamification mechanisms can substantially enhance engagement in synchronous VC environments by supporting learners’ needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness. The study contributes empirical evidence to gamification and online learning literature and offers practical guidance for educators and platform designers seeking to improve motivation, interaction, and learning quality in real-time digital instruction.

Ethical principles are essential to the responsible development and deployment of artificial intelligence (AI) in healthcare. This study examines the explicit lexical representation of predefined ethical themes in a selected corpus of 73 healthcare-AI publications. A nine-theme ethical codebook was developed from institutional guidance and relevant peer-reviewed literature. The study applied NLP-supported full-text analysis, inductive topic modeling, deductive codebook-guided content analysis, theme-based corpus analysis, and paper-level statistical comparison. The findings showed substantial variation in thematic representation. Fairness, accountability, and privacy received the strongest overall representation. Fairness had the highest raw keyword frequency, whereas accountability had the highest median adjusted occurrence rate. Transparency showed moderate representation and was mainly associated with explainability-related discussion. Patient autonomy and sustainability and environmental impact showed the weakest representation, while safety, innovation and progress, and collaboration and partnership received comparatively less attention. Friedman and Holm-adjusted pairwise analyses confirmed significant differences among themes. These findings characterize patterns of ethical-theme representation within the selected healthcare-AI literature corpus. The study proposes measurable indicators to support future healthcare-AI research, governance, and responsible system development.

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used to support academic writing in English as a Foreign Language (EFL) education. This focused narrative review critically examines selected empirical studies, research syntheses, and institutional guidance published between 2023 and 2026. It distinguishes improvements in AI-assisted texts from evidence of lasting, independent writing competence and considers feedback, critical thinking, learner autonomy, and academic integrity. The discussion incorporates emerging research from Uzbekistan while acknowledging the limited generalizability of individual institutional studies. The synthesis suggests that AI feedback can support revision when students critically evaluate suggestions, verify sources, and retain responsibility for their writing. As a conceptual contribution, the article proposes a five-stage instructional framework comprising independent planning, targeted AI assistance, critical evaluation, student-led revision, and reflection. The framework has not been empirically tested. The article concludes by identifying priorities for responsible classroom implementation and future research in Uzbek higher education.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly entering managerial decision processes, yet evidence remains fragmented regarding when AI-generated advice should be trusted, how managers should evaluate it, and how decision quality should be assessed. This study systematically reviews GenAI-supported managerial decision-making by integrating PRISMA 2020 screening, bibliometric mapping, author-keyword co-occurrence analysis, thematic synthesis, and the Theory–Context–Characteristics–Methodology (TCCM) framework. A Scopus export containing 3,500 records was screened using temporal, language, document-type, topical, and contextual criteria, yielding 99 studies published between 2024 and 2026. The final corpus comprises 342 unique authors across 94 publication sources. Four themes dominate: decision augmentation and analytics; trust, governance, and explainability; human–AI collaboration and capability; and decision quality and organizational outcomes. Trust is more often represented through governance, transparency, explainability, calibration, and human oversight than as an explicitly measured construct, while AI literacy appears explicitly in only one study. Decision quality is likewise rarely conceptualized directly and is commonly proxied by accuracy, efficiency, or predictive performance. The review proposes an integrative model in which GenAI decision-support capabilities influence managerial decision quality through calibrated trust and human–AI collaboration, with AI literacy functioning as a critical capability for verification and appropriate reliance. The study concludes with a TCCM-based research agenda for human-centered GenAI decision research. Keywords: generative AI; managerial decision-making; trust in AI; AI literacy; decision quality

documents.abstract: The current paper explores how generative artificial intelligence and algorithms change the educational process within the family. The research will explore how the technologies used in contemporary family communications, cognitive development issues, and ethical problems that arise due to the introduction of AI systems into the family learning space. Utilizing the latest theoretical approaches in pedagogical psychology, AI ethics, and family education, the research focuses on the impact of generative AI technologies, including ChatGPT, Google Gemini, and other similar technologies, on home-based learning. Based on the results of the research, the use of artificial intelligence in the learning process can have a significant effect on the ability of children to think independently and develop metacognitive skills.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly embedded in university learning, yet effective human-GenAI interaction depends not only on access to these tools but also on students' ability to formulate, evaluate, and refine prompts for academic tasks. This study examined university students' perceived GenAI prompting capability and reported prompting strategies. Questionnaire data from 234 students were analyzed using descriptive statistics, measurement modelling, scenario comparisons, structural associations, and qualitative coding of optional comments. Students reported using GenAI across diverse academic activities and generally expressed confidence in their prompting capabilities, particularly in providing relevant context and refining prompts following initial outputs. However, prompting strategies showed limited sensitivity to task types: specifying output format was more strongly endorsed in a creative workshop preparation scenario than in a research-oriented assignment, whereas other matched strategies showed no adjusted differences. Students also commonly endorsed both concise instructions and providing all relevant information at the outset, suggesting that effective brevity may depend more on selecting and organizing task-relevant information than on prompt length alone. By contrast, fixed prompt templates received lower endorsement than other prompting strategies. In the adopted factor model, perceived cognition showed the clearest unique association with perceived prompting capability, while open-ended responses highlighted prompt-intent alignment as a common challenge.

documents.abstract: Stakeholder engagement processes are structurally oriented toward human participants, leaving non-human actors such as animals and ecological systems unable to participate in the deliberative processes through which environmental decisions are negotiated. While existing approaches including ecological reports, non-human personas, and role-play have raised awareness of more-than-human concerns, they position ecological perspectives as static information rather than something stakeholders can actively engage with during deliberation. Conversational AI represents a promising but underexplored direction for enabling more dynamic, interactive forms of non-human representation in stakeholder engagement. This article investigates the design considerations and ethical boundaries shaping conversational AI systems representing more-than-human perspectives in stakeholder engagement contexts. Using koala conservation in Australia as a grounded case, we conducted a two-phase qualitative study comprising expert interviews with 22 participants across ecology, conservation, urban planning, design and AI, followed by two participatory workshops involving six and five participants, respectively. The first workshop established representational and ethical foundations, while the second examined these through interaction with a voice-based AI agent prototype. Findings reveal that more-than-human conversational agents should operate as accountable ecological proxies, grounded in local evidence and introduced early enough to shape decision-making. We derive six design considerations, including calibrated passivity as a design concept for balancing ecological advocacy with ethical restraint in future multi-stakeholder deliberation. These findings provide a foundation for designing conversational AI systems that can responsibly represent non-human interests within environmental decision-making.

documents.abstract: LLM-based agents are increasingly used to complete complex, long-horizon tasks without human intervention. To make progress toward the task goal, agents need to perform different duties, such as planning and verification, when needed. To understand how single agents manage these duties during long-horizon execution, we conduct a preliminary study. Our analysis shows that verification has the strongest association with task success, but often occurs late, leaving limited opportunities for correction. We also find that the proportion of duty-relevant information decreases as records from different duties accumulate in a shared context. These findings lead us to examine whether multi-agent systems (MAS) can address these problems by assigning duties to agents with separate contexts. Our analysis shows that this separation alone is insufficient. Agents can lose track of the overall goal and repeat prior investigations. They may also lack necessary background while receiving irrelevant information from others. To maintain goal awareness and coordinate collaboration as task needs change, we propose Goal-Aware Dynamic Multi-Agent Collaboration (GAD). It uses a growing execution graph to organize subtasks and their dependencies. To keep agents focused on their goals, each context retains the original instruction and the assigned task's goal and acceptance conditions. To adapt collaboration and information sharing during execution, agents can divide tasks into subtasks and specify dependencies based on execution evidence. These dependencies guide when agents work and which results they receive. Verification and recovery check subtask results and full task completion against their goals, providing feedback for repair when checks fail.

This presentation examines the hidden costs and long-term implications of vibe coding, an emerging approach to software development in which artificial intelligence generates software implementations from natural-language instructions with limited human review of the resulting source code. While AI-assisted coding can significantly accelerate initial software development and reduce short-term implementation costs, it may introduce substantial challenges related to code quality, technical debt, cybersecurity, software maintainability, and developer competence. The presentation explores the productivity paradox of AI-generated software, highlighting how immediate efficiency gains may be offset by increased maintenance requirements, architectural complexity, code duplication, and difficulties in understanding and modifying generated solutions. Particular attention is devoted to the accumulation of technical debt and its potential to undermine long-term software engineering productivity. Drawing on recent empirical studies and industry reports, the presentation discusses security vulnerabilities in AI-generated code, including inadequate access controls, exposure of sensitive information, and the gap between functional correctness and security compliance. It also examines the effects of AI-assisted programming on developers' learning outcomes, the unpredictability of AI service costs, and the risks of vendor lock-in. The presentation concludes by emphasizing the importance of responsible AI-assisted software development, including clear specifications, architectural guidelines, human oversight, systematic code review, rigorous testing, security verification, organizational governance, and continuous professional training.

Artificial intelligence (AI) has reached the administrative core of the universities, where students are recruited, admitted and supported. We call this administrative AI, meaning chatbots, predictive analytics and automated screening applied to administration rather than to teaching. It arrived rapidly, at an uncertain moment for higher education governance. Geopolitical upheaval is troubling student mobility and internationalisation, and universities whose finances depend on international enrolment are discovering how resilient they are. Research has been slow to follow, remaining confined to teaching and learning. Where administrative AI is noticed, it is classified as routine efficiency, far from the politics of mobility or the question of what institutions can govern. We ask three questions here. What motivates higher education institutions (HEIs) to include AI in their administrative services, and what global and geopolitical forces shape those drivers? How do such systems intersect with visa regimes, with regional education hubs, and with the financial exposure of universities that depend on international enrolment? And which governance conditions make administrative AI strengthen institutional resilience, equity and participation, and which let it erode them? Socio-technical systems theory supplies our main lens, with globalisation and diffusion research working behind it. From these perspectives we build a framework of five drivers, which are infrastructural readiness, competitive positioning under enrolment volatility, regulatory and mobility mandates, commercial platform ecosystems and sustainability legitimacy. We give each one a mechanism, a cast of actors and a characteristic risk, and different combinations direct institutions to different paths. Three socio-technical propositions organise the reading, examined against institutional cases and six documented episodes in which administrative or mobility automation failed or faced resistance. We also take up higher education as a site of soft power, automation's effect on staff as well as student mobility, and the leadership capabilities without which governance conditions stay on paper. Our central claim is that administrative AI poses a governance question rather than a merely technical one. Whether it produces resilience or dependency turns on procurement terms, contestability, who takes part, and what gets audited. The technology settles none of it.

Perkembangan pesat kecerdasan buatan (Artificial Intelligence/AI) dan otomatisasi telah mengubah secara fundamental tatanan dunia kerja, pola pendidikan, dan model pengelolaan sumber daya manusia. Fenomena disrupsi ini melahirkan tuntutan baru terhadap konsep human capital, dari sekadar modal tenaga kerja fisik menuju konsep “Human Capital 5.0” yang menekankan keselarasan antara kompetensi manusia yang berpusat pada nilai-nilai kemanusiaan (human-centered) dengan kecanggihan teknologi berbasis data (technology-based). Artikel ini bertujuan mengkaji peran pendidikan dan manajemen sumber daya manusia dalam merespons disrupsi AI dan otomatisasi, serta menganalisis kontribusi ekonomi digital dan kecerdasan buatan terhadap kualitas pengambilan keputusan bisnis. Metode yang digunakan adalah studi kepustakaan (library research) dengan pendekatan deskriptif-kualitatif terhadap literatur ilmiah nasional dan internasional. Hasil kajian menunjukkan bahwa pendidikan berperan strategis melalui reorientasi kurikulum berbasis literasi digital, penguatan pembelajaran sepanjang hayat (lifelong learning), dan pengembangan soft skill yang relatif sulit digantikan mesin; sementara manajemen sumber daya manusia berperan melalui strategi reskilling dan upskilling yang selaras dengan kebutuhan industri. Dari sisi ekonomi digital, pemanfaatan AI dan business intelligence terbukti mampu meningkatkan kecepatan, ketepatan, dan akurasi pengambilan keputusan bisnis, khususnya pada sektor Usaha Mikro, Kecil, dan Menengah (UMKM), meskipun kesenjangan akses teknologi dan literasi digital di wilayah kepulauan dan pedesaan seperti Nusa Tenggara Barat masih menjadi tantangan tersendiri. Artikel ini merekomendasikan penguatan sinergi tiga pihak (triple helix) antara lembaga pendidikan, dunia usaha, dan pemerintah daerah untuk membangun ekosistem Human Capital 5.0 yang inklusif, adaptif, dan berkelanjutan. It explores how technology can support human connection and well-being while respecting privacy, autonomy, and individual dignity. The paper proposes an ethical framework that prioritizes human dignity over excessive data collection and continuous surveillance.

documents.abstract: AI assistants are increasingly embedded in computational notebooks, scientific workflows, software engineering tools, and learning systems, yet human-AI interactions are often treated as transient prompt-response exchanges rather than durable data products, hindering reproducibility, explainability, replay, behavioral analysis, and adaptive AI support. We argue that these interactions form a new data class requiring formal representation and introduce the Human-AI Interaction Description Language (HAIDL), a formal interaction model with a Backus-Naur Form-inspired concrete syntax. HAIDL encodes each interaction as a structured object capturing computational context, user request, prompt payload, AI response, feedback, problem context, provenance, and model metadata. We integrate this vision into HAIDL-X, a middleware for JupyterLab that instantiates HAIDL by capturing user-bot state, building contextualized prompts, interfacing with AI providers, collecting feedback, and storing interactions in a repository. We add a learning layer over HAIDL that maps interaction objects and notebook execution traces into reproducible measures of user behavior, including engagement, performance, help-seeking, error-oriented use, and learning personas. HAIDL-X provides a foundation for treating human-AI collaboration as structured, queryable, replayable, analyzable data.

The digital transformation is reshaping the functioning of academic, administrative and human-resource operations in higher education institutions. The study focuses on the implementation of digital HR in the private Universities of India, specifically on the following digital HR practices: payroll automation, employee self-service, online recruitment, digital performance appraisal, learning management systems, artificial intelligence (AI), and HR analytics. The descriptive survey design was adopted and the data were obtained from 60 HR professionals and administrative personnel in private higher education institutions. The results indicate that high adoption of payroll automation and employee self-service portals and on the other hand, AI-based recruitment and HR analytics are still in their early stages. Financial challenges, employee resistance, lack of digital skills, integration of systems and data-security issues are the main challenges identified. The results have shown that the HR automation process in private Universities is moving from simple automation to more sophisticated and data-oriented HR processes; however, sophisticated digital HR is still at its beginning stage. Introduction Recent advances in Artificial intelligence (AI) and Generative AI (GenAI) have enabled more dynamic digital learning experiences. Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITSs) leverage this capability to improve learning outcomes by offering structured and responsive support. This paper introduces iLeap Tutor , an intelligent learning platform that delivers consistent, structured, course-aligned learning materials that meet course requirements, such as Course Learning Outcomes (CLOs) and National E-learning Center (NeLC) standards. Methods iLeap Tutor uses retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over the tutor's uploaded course materials together with Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite (Preview), with prompts that embed the CLO and NeLC requirements, and the tutor reviews and approves the generated course. The platform was evaluated as a single-course proof-of-concept using the Selected Topics in Computer Science course at Imam Abdulrahman Bin Faisal University (IAU). The generated content was assessed using BERTScore, Self-BLEU, and latency measurements, and thirteen academic experts evaluated the generated course in terms of content accuracy, alignment with CLOs, structure, language quality, and platform usability. Results The evaluation achieved a BERTScore-F1 of 0.829 and a cross-run Self-BLEU result of 0.553 and a within-lesson Self-BLEU of 0.146, while the generation of 16 course topics averaged 219 s in latency. At least 92.3% of responses on every questionnaire item indicated agreement, and all of them would recommend the platform. Discussion The results indicate strong semantic alignment and output consistency across multiple runs and within-lesson content diversity.
